lead: This unit joins three exam topics: energy changes and spontaneity, reaction rates and mechanisms, and phase diagrams. After it you can calculate enthalpy (ΔH), entropy (ΔS) and Gibbs free energy (ΔG), read a rate law, choose between kinetic and thermodynamic products, and apply the phase rule to water and Pb-Ag alloys.
about: This unit links three exam topics: energy and spontaneity, reaction rates and mechanisms, and phase diagrams. Chapter 3.1 builds the thermodynamic language from system definitions to ΔH, ΔS and ΔG, and bridges to cell EMF. Chapter 3.2 turns to rate laws, order and the method of initial rates. Chapter 3.3 uses energy profiles to separate fast kinetic products from stable thermodynamic products. Chapter 3.4 defines phase, component and degree of freedom and derives the phase rule. Chapters 3.5 and 3.6 apply the rule to water and to the Pb-Ag eutectic system. The advanced chapters give the minimum needed for exam diagrams and numericals.

chapters.idea: Energy changes alone do not decide spontaneity; enthalpy, entropy and free energy together do.
chapters.depth: Basic terms: system, surroundings, open, closed, isolated, homogeneous and heterogeneous; state and path functions. First law: ΔU = q + w, with q = heat and w = work. Enthalpy H = U + PV; heat capacity. Second law and entropy ΔS = q_rev/T, with q_rev = reversible heat and T = temperature in kelvin. Gibbs free energy G = H − TS; ΔG = ΔH − TΔS; spontaneity signs. Estimation of ΔH from formation or bond data and ΔS from standard values; simple numericals. Bridge to EMF: ΔG° = −nFE°, Nernst equation E = E° − (RT/nF) ln Q, where n = moles of electrons, F = Faraday constant (96500 C mol⁻¹), R = gas constant and Q = reaction quotient. Only a few universities teach the EMF part inside this unit; keep cell hardware for Unit 4.

figure.title: From energy to spontaneity
figure.aria: A downward flow from system definitions through the first law, enthalpy and entropy to Gibbs free energy and the spontaneity condition.

chapters.example: For Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s), ΔG° = −212 kJ mol⁻¹ at 298 K. Find E° and the cell EMF when [Zn²⁺] = 0.10 M and [Cu²⁺] = 1.0 M. Use n = 2 and F = 96500 C mol⁻¹. Answer: E° = −ΔG°/(nF) = 1.10 V; Q = [Zn²⁺]/[Cu²⁺] = 0.10; E = E° − (0.0592/2) log Q = 1.13 V.
chapters.trap: Using ΔH alone to predict spontaneity; the sign of ΔG decides, and ΔG = ΔH − TΔS.
chapters.leave: Cell construction, reference electrodes and battery applications go to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: A rate law turns measured concentrations into an order and a rate constant.
chapters.depth: Rate of reaction, average and instantaneous rate; rate law; order and molecularity. Zero, first and second order; integrated first-order equation ln([A]₀/[A]) = kt, with [A]₀ = initial concentration, [A] = concentration at time t and k = rate constant. Half-life t½ = 0.693/k for first order. Units of k for different overall orders. Method of initial rates. Arrhenius equation k = A e^(−Ea/RT), with A = pre-exponential factor, Ea = activation energy, R = gas constant and T = temperature in kelvin. Some syllabi call order reaction order and molecularity elementary molecularity.

figure.title: Initial rates: [A]₀, [B]₀, rate ×10³
figure.aria: Three initial-rate trials: doubling A quadruples the rate, while doubling B leaves the rate unchanged.

chapters.example: For A + B → products, the initial rates are: Trial 1, [A]₀ = 0.10 M, [B]₀ = 0.10 M, rate = 2.0 × 10⁻³ mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹; Trial 2, [A]₀ = 0.20 M, [B]₀ = 0.10 M, rate = 8.0 × 10⁻³ mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹; Trial 3, [A]₀ = 0.10 M, [B]₀ = 0.20 M, rate = 2.0 × 10⁻³ mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹. Find the order in A, the order in B, the overall order and k. Answer: order in A = 2; order in B = 0; overall order = 2; k = rate/[A]² = 0.20 L mol⁻¹ s⁻¹.
chapters.trap: Confusing order with stoichiometric coefficient, or forgetting that a zero-order reactant can still appear in the balanced equation.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 3.1 for energy changes; basic concentration units.
chapters.leave: Mechanism and product control go to Chapter 3.3; reactor design is outside this book.

chapters.idea: The fastest product is not always the most stable product; temperature chooses between them.
chapters.depth: Elementary steps, molecularity, rate-determining step and the steady-state approximation for intermediates. Energy profile and activation energy. Kinetic product: forms faster, lower Ea. Thermodynamic product: more stable, lower Gibbs free energy. Trapping of reactive intermediates. Effect of temperature and catalyst. Some syllabi call this product control or kinetic versus thermodynamic control. Use simple energy profiles; do not drift into named organic syntheses.

figure.aria: Two energy profiles from the same reactant: the fast route has a 60 kJ mol⁻¹ barrier to B, the slow route has a 90 kJ mol⁻¹ barrier to C, and C ends 20 kJ mol⁻¹ lower.

chapters.example: For A → B, Ea = 60 kJ mol⁻¹. For A → C, Ea = 90 kJ mol⁻¹. Product C is 20 kJ mol⁻¹ more stable than B. At low temperature and at high temperature, which product is favoured? Answer: at low temperature B is favoured by kinetic control because it forms faster; at high temperature C is favoured by thermodynamic control because it is more stable.
chapters.trap: Saying lower activation energy means a more stable product. Lower Ea means faster, not necessarily more stable.
chapters.leave: Named organic reactions and stereochemistry belong to an organic chemistry course; here keep the energy-profile logic.

chapters.idea: The phase rule counts how many intensive variables a system can change without losing a phase.
chapters.depth: Definitions: phase P = a physically distinct homogeneous part; component C = minimum number of independent chemical species needed to describe all phases; degree of freedom F = number of independent intensive variables. Derivation of Gibbs phase rule F = C − P + 2. Reduced phase rule F = C − P + 1 at constant pressure. Worked F for systems with reaction. Only a few universities teach the derivation in full; others use the result.

figure.aria: A box tree with the phase rule as root and three branches for components, phases, and the two intensive variables.

chapters.example: For CaCO₃(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO₂(g), find C, P and F at equilibrium. Answer: species = 3; independent reaction = 1; C = 3 − 1 = 2. Phases = solid CaCO₃, solid CaO and gas CO₂, so P = 3. F = C − P + 2 = 2 − 3 + 2 = 1. At fixed pressure the reduced rule gives F = 2 − 3 + 1 = 0.
chapters.trap: Counting every chemical species as a component; a reaction reduces C.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 3.1 for state functions; basic chemical equilibrium.
chapters.leave: Full alloy diagrams go to Chapter 3.6; water hardness and treatment go to Unit 7.

chapters.idea: Water's three phase boundaries meet at a unique triple point and end at a critical point.
chapters.depth: One-component system for water. Phase regions: ice, liquid water and vapour. Curves: sublimation, fusion and vaporization. Triple point at 273.16 K and 611 Pa. Critical point at 647 K and 22.1 MPa. F values from the phase rule. Negative slope of the fusion curve and why pressure lowers the melting point of ice. Only a few universities teach the full diagram; keep it schematic with these numbers.

figure.aria: Schematic pressure–temperature phase diagram for water; the three curves meet at the triple point near 273.16 K and 0.611 kPa and end at the critical point near 647 K and 22.1 MPa.

chapters.example: Water has a triple point at 273.16 K and 611 Pa. Find F at the triple point and along the liquid-vapour curve. Answer: C = 1. At the triple point P = 3, so F = 1 − 3 + 2 = 0. Along the liquid-vapour curve P = 2, so F = 1 − 2 + 2 = 1.
chapters.trap: Calling 273.15 K and 1 atm the triple point; that is the normal melting point, not the triple point.
chapters.leave: Alloy phase diagrams go to Chapter 3.6; water hardness and treatment go to Unit 7.

chapters.idea: The Pb-Ag system shows a simple eutectic where the reduced phase rule gives zero freedom.
chapters.depth: Reduced phase rule F = C − P + 1 at constant pressure. Two-component Pb-Ag simple eutectic system. Eutectic at 303 °C and 2.5 mass% Ag. Regions: primary Pb, primary Ag, liquid, liquid + solid, and eutectic mixture. Liquidus, solidus, tie line and lever rule. Cooling curves. F in one-phase, two-phase and eutectic points. Some syllabi add compound formation with congruent melting and Zn-Mg; mention only the definition, not a full diagram. Only a few universities teach this phase diagram.

figure.aria: Schematic Pb-Ag temperature–composition diagram with a eutectic at 303 °C and 2.5 mass% Ag; a 5 mass% Ag alloy is marked by a vertical line.

chapters.example: The Pb-Ag phase diagram has a eutectic at 303 °C and 2.5 mass% Ag. An alloy is made from 5.0 g Ag and 95.0 g Pb. Find its mass% Ag, whether it is hypo- or hyper-eutectic, F at the eutectic with liquid and both solids present, and F in the liquid region at 400 °C. Answer: mass% Ag = 5.0%, so it is hyper-eutectic. At the eutectic P = 3, C = 2, reduced F = 2 − 3 + 1 = 0. At 400 °C the alloy is all liquid, P = 1, reduced F = 2 − 1 + 1 = 2.
chapters.trap: Using F = C − P + 2 for an alloy at fixed pressure; use the reduced rule F = C − P + 1.
chapters.leave: Compound formation with congruent melting and Zn-Mg details go to a materials course; corrosion of metals goes to Unit 4.

links: ΔG says if; rate law says how fast
rate law gives the rate-determining step
ΔG separates stable from fast products
